title: Some Kids Will Never Think AI Is Cool
gist: A short piece (the text available is the opening of the article, cut off before the reported interviews) documenting that US teens are adopting AI while actively disliking it: YPulse finds 37 percent of 13-to-17-year-olds cringe at AI-generated content and more than half worry about misinformation and deepfakes, while Pew finds over a quarter expect AI to harm society over the next 20 years. A communications professor argues the backlash is unusual because it comes from the young rather than from older generations.

insights.claim: Market research firm YPulse finds that 37 percent of US teens aged 13 to 17 cringe when they see AI-generated content such as music and videos, and more than half worry about misinformation and deepfakes.
insights.speaker: Elana Klein
insights.so_what: Quantifies brand toxicity of visible AI-generated content with the demographic that sets consumer taste — a risk for AI-forward media and advertising products.
insights.locator: according to market research firm YPulse

insights.claim: A recent Pew Research report finds many teens think AI will be good for them personally, yet over a fourth of the cohort believe AI will have a negative impact on society over the next 20 years, citing job loss, decline of critical thinking, and environmental impacts.
insights.speaker: Elana Klein
insights.so_what: The personal-versus-societal split is where regulatory support originates: users can keep using a product while voting against it.
insights.locator: A recent Pew Research report found that while many teens

insights.claim: High teen adoption of chatbots coexists with mixed enthusiasm, meaning usage metrics substantially overstate affinity for AI products among young people.
insights.speaker: Elana Klein
insights.so_what: Engagement numbers from this cohort are a weak proxy for durable loyalty or willingness to pay.
insights.quote: The polling on youthful AI attitudes shows a great deal of contradiction.
insights.locator: The polling on youthful AI attitudes

insights.claim: Unlike previous consumer technologies that young people adopted eagerly, the moral panic around AI is not coming from older generations — kids are turned off by AI being pushed on them by adults and tech corporations, according to University at Buffalo communications professor Melanie Green.
insights.speaker: Elana Klein
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual adoption dynamic: top-down corporate push is generating resistance rather than aspiration in the key demographic.
insights.locator: Young people typically adopt new consumer technology eagerly

insights.claim: Teen resistance is rooted in a perception of asymmetric exposure — Green says they are acutely aware their generation will bear the brunt of whatever disruption AI causes.
insights.speaker: Elana Klein
insights.so_what: A grievance framed around labor-market displacement is durable and likely to translate into political pressure as this cohort ages into voting.
insights.quote: acutely aware that whatever disruption happens, their generation is going to be bearing the brunt of it.

insights.claim: AI has become a cultural shorthand for fakery among young people, with parents on Bluesky reporting children say 'that's AI' to mean 'that's BS,' and educators on Reddit reporting students who use AI still cannot stand the art it produces.
insights.speaker: Elana Klein
insights.so_what: When a technology's name becomes a pejorative, AI-branding on consumer products shifts from an asset to a liability.
insights.locator: On Bluesky, parents bond over their kids’ distrust of AI
